4. In support of his submission that the petitioner illegally impleaded the Returning Officer and Assistant Returning Officer in the Election Petition the learned Advocate placed reliance in the case of Mohan Raj vs. Surendra Kumar Taparia and others, reported in AIR 1969 (SC) 677, wherein it has been held that when the Act makes a person necessary party and provides that the petition shall be dismissed if such a party is not joined/the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be used as curative means to save the Election Petition. In that case under the Indian Election Rules some persons were to be made parties but in the Election petition those persons were not made parties. Subsequently, an objection was raised as to non joinder of necessary parties and an application was filed for amendment of the Election petition under the provision of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Indian Supreme Court has held that such power of amendment is not available to the Election Tribunal and the petition was rightly dismissed for non joinder of the parties who are necessary parties. The facts mentioned in the case and the facts of the case before us are distinctly different. On the same point there is another decision of Indian Supreme Court, reported in AIR (1976) 744 Udhay Singh vs. Madhav Rao Scindia which is also a case of non joinder of necessary parties. The learned Advocates for the petitioner also placed reliance in the case of Satya Narain vs. Dhuja Ram and others, reported in AIR (1974) SC) 1185, wherein the Supreme Court held that the Election petition cannot be equated with a plaint in a civil suit. In the case copies of the Election petition were not enclosed with the summons for serving upon the respondents to enable quick despatch of the notice with contents of the allegations. The Supreme Court has held that the Registrar or the Deputy Registrar has not been conferred with any power to permit correction or removal of defects in an Election petition presented in the High Court beyond period of limitation. The learned Advocate for the petitioner then placed reliance in the case of Jyoti Basu and others vs. Debi Ghosal and others, reported in AIR 1982 (SC) 983 wherein it has been held that no one may be joined as a party to an election petition otherwise than as provided by sections 82 and 86(4) of the Indian Act. It follows that a person who is not a candidate may be joined as a respondent to the election petition. It has further been held that it is as if a person guilty of a corrupt practice can get away with it. Where at the concluding stage of the trial of an election petition, after evidence has been given, the court finds that there is sufficient material to hold a person guilty of a corrupt practice, the court may then issue a notice to him to show cause under section 99 and proceed with further action. Relying on these four decisions the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Tribunal committed wrong and illegality in rejecting the petitioner's prayer for dismissal of the election petition on the ground, of non compliance of Articles 30 and 51 (2) of the aforesaid Order. 

 5. Article 50 of the Order provides that the petitioner shall join as respondents to his election petition all contesting candidates, and any other candidate against whom any allegation, if any, of any corrupt or illegal practice is made and shall serve personally or by registered post on each such respondent a copy of his petition. In the present case the petitioner has impleaded the Returning Officer and Assistant Returning Officer as respondents in the Election petition in addition to others. It is submitted that they are unnecessary parties. Article 51 (2) provides that a petitioner may claim as relief any of the declarations, that the election of the returned candidate is void; and that the petitioner or some other person has been duly elected; or that the election as a whole is void. The learned Advocate contends that in the present election petition these two provisions of the Order has not been scrupulously followed which is mandatory. The learned Advocate has drawn our attention to the provision of Articles 58 Of the Order which provides that the Tribunal shall dismiss an election petition, if the provisions of Articles 50 of Articles 51 have not been complied with including clauss 4(c) of Articles 57, The second part of Article 58 is not applicable in this petition before us. It appears from the election petition that the petitioner has impleaded all the contesting candidates and in addition to that he has impleaded the Returning Officer and the Assistant Returning Officer and according to the learned Advocate this impleading of Returning Officer and Assistant Returning Officer is against the provision of Article 50 of the Order. When the petitioner has impleaded all the necessary parties mere impleading the Returning Officer and the Assistant Returning Officer or so to say misjoinder of these the petitioners cannot by itself be a ground for holding that there was total non compliance of the provision of Article 50 of the Order. Furthermore, in the election petition there are specific allegations of corrupt practice against these two officers. As regards the allegations of non compliance of Articles 81(2) of the Order we have gone through the prayer portion of the election petition and we find nothing wrong in it.  7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his submission referred the aforesaid decisions of the Indian jurisdiction. We have gone through these decisions and we are of the view that these have no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present application. These decisions are based on non-joinder of necessary parties. The provision of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 is very much silent on the mis-joinder of parties. From the provision of this Order it cannot be found that if any unnecessary party is impleaded that can be a. ground for rejection of the election petition when there is compliance of other provision and when in the present case the petitioner impleaded all the necessary parties the mere fact that some other persons have been made parties in the election petition by itself cannot be a ground for rejection of the election petition.
